meta.title: Embeddings as Learned Representations
meta.thesis: An embedding is a learned vector that turns the meaning of a word, sentence, or item into coordinates, so similarity becomes a distance you can search, rank, and validate.

mentalMap.caption: These five ideas relate; start anywhere, but the spine reads left to right.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: An embedding is a learned vector that places similar things near each other, so meaning becomes math you can search and compare.

nodes.label: What an embedding is
nodes.sub: A vector that turns meaning into coordinates you can measure.
nodes.orient: What an embedding is and why raw text or IDs cannot be compared by meaning.
nodes.what: An embedding is a fixed-length vector of numbers that represents the meaning of a thing.
nodes.relevance: It matters because once meaning is a vector, similarity becomes a distance you can compute.

nodes.label: How it is learned
nodes.sub: Training nudges vectors so context predicts neighbours.
nodes.orient: How a model learns vectors from data so that similar items land close together.
nodes.what: Embeddings are learned by training a model to predict context, pulling related items together.
nodes.relevance: It matters because 'learned' is the difference between geometry that means something and random numbers.

nodes.label: Choices that shape them
nodes.sub: Dimension, model, and distance metric trade cost for quality.
nodes.orient: The design choices (dimensions, model, similarity metric) that change quality, cost, and risk.
nodes.what: Embedding dimension, source model, and distance metric are the levers you actually choose.
nodes.relevance: It matters because the same text gives different results depending on these choices.

nodes.relevance: It matters because semantic search and retrieval are just nearest-neighbour lookups over embeddings.

modules.title: What an embedding is
modules.sub: Starts the spine: the problem embeddings solve.
modules.summary: Build the simplest useful picture of an embedding: a learned vector that turns the meaning of a word, sentence, or item into coordinates you can measure. This module answers what an embedding is and why we need one.
objectives: Explain an embedding as a fixed-length vector that places similar things near each other.
Say why raw text or ID numbers cannot be compared by meaning, but embeddings can.
Name one decision embeddings change: how you search or group items by meaning.

blocks.title: What an embedding is, and the problem it solves
blocks.analogy: An embedding is like a postcode for meaning: things that mean similar things get nearby coordinates, so you can find neighbours by looking at who is close.

spans.text: Before reading on, predict:
how could a computer tell that "car" and "automobile" mean almost the same thing, when the letters are completely different?

Computers store words as text and items as ID numbers. Neither can be compared by meaning: the strings "car" and "automobile" share no letters, and item #4012 is not "closer" to #4013 just because the numbers are adjacent. We need a representation where distance means similarity.
An
embedding
is that representation: a fixed-length list of numbers (a vector) that an
ai
model produces for a word, sentence, image, or product. Similar things get vectors that point in similar directions, so meaning becomes geometry you can measure.

items.text: Input: a piece of content (a word, sentence, or item). Output: a vector, e.g. 384 numbers.
"Similar" means the two vectors are close — small angle, high cosine similarity.
The decision it changes: you can now search and group by meaning, not by exact keywords.

blocks.title: From letters to coordinates
blocks.caption: Slide to see how content is turned into a vector you can compare.

steps.label: Raw content
steps.detail: A word, sentence, or item — "a small electric car". Just text; no notion of similarity yet.

steps.label: Tokenize
steps.detail: The model splits the text into tokens it recognises from training.

steps.label: Embed
steps.detail: The model maps the tokens to one fixed-length vector, e.g. [0.12, -0.04, 0.91, ...].

steps.label: Compare
steps.detail: Two vectors can now be scored by closeness; "car" lands near "vehicle", far from "banana".

blocks.title: Reading an embedding by hand

spans.text: Take "dog", "puppy", and "calculator". Your intuition already says the first two are close in meaning.
A good embedding gives "dog" and "puppy" vectors that point in nearly the same direction, while "calculator" points elsewhere.
Cosine similarity returns about 0.8 for dog/puppy and about 0.1 for dog/calculator. The number, not the spelling, captures meaning.

blocks.title: Where you have already met embeddings

spans.text: When a shopping site shows "customers also viewed" or a help search finds the right article even though you used different words, embeddings are usually behind it. Each product or article was embedded once; your query is embedded live and matched to the nearest vectors.
The takeaway pattern: embed your items once, store the vectors, then compare any new input against them by distance.

blocks.title: What lives inside the vector

spans.text: Each number in the vector is a dimension the model learned during training. No single dimension means "is an animal" in a human-readable way; meaning is spread across all of them. That is why embeddings are called distributed representations.
You never set the numbers by hand. The model produces them, and you only compare them — which is exactly why we say embeddings are learned.

blocks.prompt: Why can't a computer compare the words "car" and "automobile" by meaning before embedding them?

options.text: The two words share no letters, so string comparison sees them as unrelated.
Computers cannot store text at all.
Because "automobile" is a longer word, it is always ranked lower.

blocks.explanation: Raw text and ID numbers carry no notion of meaning-distance. An embedding maps both words to nearby vectors so similarity becomes measurable.

modules.title: How embeddings are learned
modules.sub: Follows module 1 — explains where the meaningful vectors come from.
modules.summary: See where the numbers come from: a model is trained so that things appearing in similar contexts get similar vectors. This is what "learned" means and why the geometry carries meaning instead of being random.
objectives: Explain that embeddings are learned by training a model to predict context.
Describe how a loss function pulls related items together and pushes unrelated ones apart.
Connect 'learned' to generalization: unseen but similar inputs still land nearby.

blocks.title: Where the meaningful numbers come from
blocks.analogy: Learning embeddings is like seating people at a wedding by who they keep being seen with: friends drift to the same table, strangers end up far apart — nobody assigns seats by hand.

spans.text: Before reading on, predict:
if nobody hand-writes the numbers, what signal in plain text could a model use to decide that "king" and "queen" belong near each other?
The signal is context. Words that appear in similar surroundings tend to mean similar things — "king" and "queen" both show up near "throne", "royal", "reign". A
ml
model is trained to predict the context of an item, and the vectors that make those predictions easy end up encoding meaning.
During training a
loss

score measures how wrong each prediction is. The model adjusts vectors to lower the loss, which pulls items that share context together and pushes unrelated items apart. Run this over a huge corpus and the geometry settles into something meaningful.

items.text: Input to training: lots of real text or item sequences. Output: one vector per item.
The model never sees "car means vehicle" stated; it infers it from shared context.
This is why it is a learned representation, not a hand-coded lookup table.

blocks.title: One training step, in slow motion

spans.text: The model reads "the cat sat on the ___" and must predict the missing word from the current vectors.
It guesses "car"; the real word was "mat". The loss is high because the guess was far off.
It shifts the vectors a little so "mat" becomes more likely next time. Repeat billions of times and similar contexts produce similar vectors.

blocks.title: The famous king - man + woman example

spans.text: Because relationships are encoded as directions, you can do arithmetic on the vectors. Taking the vector for "king", subtracting "man", and adding "woman" lands you very close to the vector for "queen".
No one programmed that rule. It fell out of training on context — which is the whole point of calling embeddings learned representations.

blocks.title: Why training generalizes to new inputs

spans.text: Because the model learns from patterns of context rather than memorizing exact strings, it achieves
generalization
: a word or sentence it has rarely seen still lands near related ones, as long as it appeared in similar contexts. That is what lets embeddings handle paraphrases and typos gracefully.
Rule of thumb: if two inputs would be used interchangeably in real text, a well-trained embedding places them close — even if you never saw that exact pair during training.

blocks.prompt: What does it mean that embeddings are "learned" rather than hand-coded?

options.text: An engineer types the vector for every word by hand.
A model adjusts the vectors during training so items in similar contexts end up close.
The numbers are random and never change.

blocks.explanation: Training uses a loss signal to pull items that share context together, so the geometry encodes meaning the model was never explicitly told.

modules.title: Choices that shape your embeddings
modules.sub: Follows module 2 — now you pick the knobs that change the result.
modules.summary: The same text gives different vectors depending on three choices: which model produces them, how many dimensions they have, and which distance metric scores similarity. This module makes those tradeoffs concrete so you choose deliberately.
objectives: Name the three levers: source model, embedding dimension, and similarity metric.
Pick a sensible default and say when a bigger or specialized model is worth the cost.
Recognize the failure mode of mixing vectors from different models in one index.

blocks.title: The three levers you actually choose

spans.text: You rarely train embeddings yourself; you call a
model
that produces them. But you still make three decisions that change quality, cost, and risk.

items.text: Source model: a small general model (cheap, fast) vs a large or domain-tuned one (better on jargon, costlier).
Dimension: more dimensions can capture more nuance but cost more memory and search time. 384 or 768 are common defaults.
Similarity metric: cosine similarity is the usual default; it ignores vector length and compares direction (meaning).

spans.text: The trap: these are not free choices that you can mix later. Every vector in one search index must come from the same model and dimension, or the distances become meaningless.

blocks.title: Choosing for a real project

spans.text: Pick a small, well-known general model (for example a 384-dimension sentence model) and cosine similarity. It works surprisingly often.
Only reach for a larger or domain-tuned model after you can show the default misses real queries — otherwise you pay more for no gain.
Record the model name and dimension next to your stored vectors so you never accidentally mix two models in one index.

blocks.title: Which embedding model should you reach for?

options.name: Small general model (~384 dims)

cells.text: Good for everyday text, search, and prototypes.
Cheap to run; can embed locally.
May miss specialized jargon or long documents.

options.whenToUse: Start here for almost any first build.

options.name: Large hosted model (~1536 dims)

cells.text: Stronger on nuance and longer text.
Per-call cost and an API dependency.
More memory and slower search at scale.

options.whenToUse: Use when the small model demonstrably misses real queries.

options.name: Domain-tuned model

cells.text: Best on niche vocabulary (legal, medical, code).

options.whenToUse: Use only after measuring that general models fail on your domain.

blocks.howToRead: Pick the smallest model that passes your similarity test; upgrade only on measured evidence.

blocks.title: How embedding choices break in practice

spans.text: Bad similarity results usually trace back to a choice made here, not to the math.
The three most common ways it goes wrong:
1. Mixed models in one index
You re-embed half your items with a new model. Old and new vectors live in different spaces, so distances are nonsense and results look random. Always re-embed the whole
pipeline
when you change models.
2. Wrong metric for the vectors
Using raw Euclidean distance on vectors meant for cosine similarity lets long vectors dominate, so popular-but-irrelevant items rank first.
3. Chasing dimensions
More dimensions feels safer but multiplies memory and search cost while often adding little quality. Pick a default and only grow it on evidence.

blocks.prompt: You add new items to a search index using a different embedding model than the existing items. What happens?

options.text: Nothing — embeddings are interchangeable across models.
The new and old vectors are in different spaces, so similarity scores become meaningless.
The index automatically converts the new vectors to match.

blocks.explanation: Vectors are only comparable within the same model and dimension. Changing models means re-embedding everything in the index.

modules.decisionItForces: Choose the right level of rigor for Embeddings as Learned Representations: baseline, production design, or advanced optimization.

modules.title: Using embeddings in code
modules.sub: Follows module 3 — turn the chosen model into a working search.
modules.summary: Put it together: embed your items once, embed an incoming query, and rank items by cosine similarity. That three-step shape is the core of semantic search and retrieval, and it is only a few lines of code.
objectives: Read a minimal embed-then-rank pipeline and predict its output.
Identify the line that decides which item is most similar to a query.
List what to verify before trusting AI-generated embedding code.

blocks.title: The embed-once, query-live pattern

spans.text: Almost every use of embeddings is the same three-step shape, run by an
ai
model:

items.text: Embed your items once and store the vectors (this is your search index).
When a query arrives, embed it live with the same model.
Rank the stored items by similarity to the query vector and return the top few.

spans.text: That is semantic search. The same shape powers retrieval for chatbots, recommendations, and deduplication — only the items change.

blocks.title: Tracing one query through the code

spans.text: Each document string is turned into a vector and kept in a list, paired with its text.
The query "a feline pet" is embedded with the same model, so it lands in the same space as the documents.
Cosine similarity scores every document; the highest score wins. "A cat is a small pet" beats "The stock market fell" even with no shared keywords.

blocks.title: What a result looks like

spans.text: Query: "a feline pet". Even though none of those words appear in the documents, the ranked output is: "A cat is a small pet" (0.71), "Dogs are loyal animals" (0.39), "The stock market fell" (0.04).
Notice the top hit shares zero keywords with the query — it wins purely on meaning. That is the payoff of embeddings over exact-match search.

blocks.title: Semantic search in a dozen lines
blocks.code:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")  # 384-dim general model
docs = ["A cat is a small pet", "Dogs are loyal animals", "The stock market fell"]

doc_vecs = model.encode(docs)              # embed items ONCE
query_vec = model.encode("a feline pet")   # embed the query LIVE

scores = util.cos_sim(query_vec, doc_vecs)[0]  # cosine similarity to each doc
best = scores.argmax()
print(docs[best], float(scores[best]))

spans.text: Same model for docs and query, store the doc vectors once, and let cosine similarity pick the closest. Swap in any list of items and you have semantic search.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before running it: which document will this print, and roughly what score — given the query "a feline pet"?
predictThenReveal.answer: It prints "A cat is a small pet" with a score around 0.7. "feline" and "cat" are near each other in the embedding space, so that doc has the highest cosine similarity even though it shares no words with the query.

syntax.explains: Turns text into vectors; must be the same model for docs and query.
Picks the index of the highest-scoring document.

spans.text: When an AI writes embedding code for you, check these before trusting it:

items.text: Does it use the SAME model to embed the documents and the query? A mismatch silently returns garbage.
Does it use cosine similarity (or normalize first) rather than raw Euclidean distance on un-normalized vectors?
Does it embed the items once and reuse the stored vectors, not re-embed on every query?
Does it handle an empty or out-of-domain query without crashing or returning a confident-but-wrong top hit?
Sanity check: run two inputs you KNOW are similar and confirm they score high.

blocks.prompt: In the semantic-search code, which line decides which document is the best match?

options.text: model.encode(docs) — embedding the documents.
scores.argmax() — picking the highest cosine-similarity score.
SentenceTransformer(...) — loading the model.

blocks.explanation: Encoding produces the vectors and cos_sim scores them, but argmax is what selects the single closest document to return.

modules.title: Where embeddings break, and how to check
modules.sub: Closes the spine — recall the idea, then validate before trusting it.
modules.summary: Embeddings fail quietly: a wrong-but-confident similarity score looks just like a right one. This module recalls the core idea, names the realistic failure modes, and gives you a validation habit using labelled pairs.
objectives: Recall, from memory, what makes a representation 'learned' and why distance equals similarity.
Name how embeddings break: stale vectors, model drift, and out-of-domain inputs.
Choose a validation rigor and run a labelled-pair check before trusting results.

blocks.title: Quick recall: what did the first two modules establish?

spans.text: Before reading on, predict:
from memory — what makes a representation "learned", and why does closeness between two vectors mean the items are similar?
Module 1: an embedding turns meaning into a vector, so similarity becomes a distance — high cosine similarity means close in meaning. Module 2: those vectors are
learned
by training a
model
to predict context, which is why the geometry carries meaning instead of being arbitrary.
Hold both ideas: the danger is that a vector always returns a confident distance, even when the embedding is the wrong tool or has gone stale. So we validate.

blocks.title: A validation habit you can reuse

spans.text: Write 10-20 pairs you KNOW should be similar and a few you know should not. This is your ground truth.
Confirm the should-be-similar pairs score higher than the should-be-different ones. If not, your model or metric is wrong for this data.
Changed the model, dimension, or re-indexed? Run the same labelled set again. A silent drop here is your early warning of a broken pipeline.

blocks.title: How much validation does this use deserve?

options.name: Eyeball a few queries

cells.text: Fine for a prototype or demo.
Almost none — just look at results.
Misses systematic errors you didn't think to test.

options.whenToUse: Use while you are still exploring whether embeddings even help.

options.name: Labelled-pair test

cells.text: Catches most real failures before users do.
Write 10-20 pairs once; re-run on change.
Low if the pairs reflect real usage.

options.whenToUse: Use for anything users will actually depend on.

options.name: Monitored retrieval metrics

cells.text: Best for high-stakes or large-scale search.
Needs logging, recall@k tracking, and alerts.

options.whenToUse: Use when wrong results cost money, safety, or trust.

blocks.howToRead: Pick the lightest check that would catch a failure your users would actually notice.

blocks.title: The quiet ways embeddings drift

spans.text: Embeddings rarely throw an error when they go wrong. Watch for these silent failures:

items.text: Stale vectors: items were edited but never re-embedded, so search points at the old meaning.
Model drift: you upgraded the embedding model but did not re-embed the whole index.
Out-of-domain input: a general model embeds niche jargon poorly and still returns a confident-looking score.

spans.text: A labelled-pair test run on every deploy turns all three of these from silent disasters into a visible, failing check.

blocks.prompt: Why are embedding failures considered especially dangerous?

options.text: They always crash the program, halting everything.
They return a confident similarity score even when the result is wrong, so the error is silent.
They cannot be tested in any way.

blocks.explanation: A wrong-but-confident score looks identical to a correct one. That is why you validate with labelled pairs rather than trusting the number.

modules.decisionItForces: Choose how much validation an embedding use deserves: eyeball it, a labelled-pair test, or monitored retrieval metrics.

ai.label: AI
ai.laymanDefinition: Systems that perform tasks associated with human intelligence.
ai.technicalNote: Here, an AI model is what produces the embedding vectors you search and compare.

ml.label: ML
ml.laymanDefinition: AI systems that learn from data.
ml.technicalNote: Embeddings are an ML output: the vectors are learned from data rather than written by hand.

model.label: Model
model.laymanDefinition: The trained program that turns content into an embedding vector.
model.technicalNote: An embedding model maps inputs to a fixed-length vector; the same model must embed both stored items and queries.

loss.label: Loss
loss.laymanDefinition: A score of how wrong the model's prediction was, which training tries to lower.
loss.technicalNote: During training, lowering the loss nudges vectors so items sharing context move closer together.

generalization.label: Generalization
generalization.laymanDefinition: Doing well on inputs the model never saw during training.
generalization.technicalNote: Because embeddings learn from context patterns, similar-but-unseen inputs still land near related ones.

pipeline.label: Pipeline
pipeline.laymanDefinition: The end-to-end flow: embed items, store vectors, embed query, rank by similarity.
pipeline.technicalNote: If any stage uses a different model or dimension than the rest, distances stop being comparable.

questions.q: Do you need to match items by meaning rather than exact keywords?
questions.why: Embeddings earn their cost only when keyword matching is too brittle for your queries.
opts: Maybe — prototype with a small model first
questions.rot: Start with the smallest model and a labelled-pair test before scaling up.

spans.text: Close the book for a moment and reconstruct the chain from memory:
What is an embedding? Why is it called learned? Which three choices shape it? What three steps turn it into search? And how do you check it before trusting it?

If you can answer those without peeking, you hold the whole lesson: meaning becomes a vector, training makes that geometry meaningful, model/dimension/metric are your levers, embed-then-rank is the pattern, and a labelled-pair test is the guardrail.

capstone.prompt: Solo build: take 20 short documents of your own, embed them with a small sentence model, and write a function that returns the 3 most similar to any query using cosine similarity. Then add a labelled-pair test of 5 known-similar and 5 known-different pairs and confirm the ordering holds. NEXT RUNG: store the vectors in a vector database (e.g. FAISS or a hosted index) and feed the top results into an LLM prompt — that is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), the natural next lesson.

finalCheck.title: Knowledge check
finalCheck.intro: A quick check across the whole lesson — pick or type your answers.

questions.prompt: Raw text like the word 'cat' and an ID number like 42 both fail at the same job. What can embeddings do that those representations cannot?

options.text: Store the original text so it can be retrieved later
Place items with similar meaning close together in a numeric space so they can be compared
Compress files to save disk space
Translate text between languages automatically

questions.explanation: Embeddings encode meaning as a fixed-length vector, so items that are semantically similar end up geometrically close — something raw text strings and arbitrary ID numbers cannot do.

questions.prompt: During training, a loss function shapes what the embedding space looks like. Which statement best describes what it does?

options.text: It randomly shuffles vectors so the model doesn't memorise the training data
It pulls vectors for related items closer together and pushes vectors for unrelated items further apart
It sets the embedding dimension to the optimal size automatically
It converts embeddings back into readable text for evaluation

questions.explanation: The loss function is the training signal that makes the geometry meaningful — rewarding closeness for related pairs and penalising it for unrelated ones.

questions.prompt: You have two embedding indexes: one built with Model A and one built with Model B. A colleague suggests merging them into a single index to simplify search. What is the key risk?

options.text: The combined index will be too large to fit in memory
Vectors from different models live in incompatible spaces, so distance comparisons become meaningless
Cosine similarity stops working once an index exceeds a certain size
The embedding dimension will automatically double, slowing down queries

questions.explanation: Each model learns its own coordinate system; mixing vectors from different models is like mixing measurements in metres and miles — the numbers are incomparable.

questions.prompt: In a minimal embed-then-rank pipeline, what is the role of the single line that computes similarity scores between the query vector and every item vector?
questions.acceptableAnswer: That line compares the query embedding to each stored embedding (typically using cosine similarity or dot product) and produces a score for each item, so the highest-scoring item can be returned as the most similar result.
questions.explanation: The similarity computation is the decision point of the pipeline — it is what converts raw vectors into a ranked list, making it the line that determines which item wins.

questions.prompt: Your embedding-powered search worked great at launch, but six months later users complain it returns irrelevant results. Which combination of failure modes should you investigate first?

options.text: Embedding dimension too small and cosine similarity chosen over dot product
Stale vectors (new content never re-embedded) and out-of-domain inputs (new topics the model never saw)
The loss function was not reset after deployment
The index was built with too many items, causing distance scores to saturate

questions.explanation: Stale vectors and out-of-domain inputs are the two most common causes of embedding quality degrading over time — content changes and user language shifts can both silently break retrieval.
